what_its_for: Estradiol is a form of estrogen, a female hormone. It is used to treat symptoms of menopause such as hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, itching, and burning. It may also be used to prevent bone loss (osteoporosis) after menopause, treat certain hormone-related conditions, and in transgender women as part of hormone therapy.
how_to_take: How you take estradiol depends on the form your doctor prescribed. PILLS: Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water, with or without food, at the same time every day. PATCH: Apply to clean, dry, hairless skin on your lower belly or buttocks. Press firmly for 10 seconds. Change the patch as directed (usually once or twice a week). Do not apply to your breasts or irritated skin. Rotate the location each time. GEL or SPRAY: Apply to clean, dry skin on your arm, thigh, or as directed. Let it dry completely before covering with clothing. Wash your hands right away after applying. Do not let others touch the area where you applied the gel or spray. VAGINAL CREAM or TABLET: Use the applicator provided to place the medication inside your vagina as directed by your doctor. VAGINAL RING: Your doctor or nurse will insert the flexible ring into your vagina. It stays in place for 90 days and then needs to be replaced.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe the lowest dose that works for you. Doses vary depending on the form and what it is being used for. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not change your dose on your own. Use this medication at the same time each day or on the same days each week to help you remember.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it or apply it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Never double up to make up for a missed dose. For patches: if you forget to change your patch on the scheduled day, change it as soon as you remember and then continue on your original schedule. If needed, set a phone reminder to help you remember your doses.
storage: Store tablets and patches at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep medications out of the reach of children and pets. Do not store in the bathroom. For gels and creams, follow the storage instructions on the package label. Used patches still contain active medication — fold them in half with the sticky sides together and dispose of them safely in the trash, away from children and pets. Do not flush patches down the toilet.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking while taking estradiol — smoking significantly increases the risk of serious side effects such as blood clots, stroke, and heart attack. Do not let other people, especially children or men, come into contact with the area where you applied estradiol gel or spray, as it can be absorbed through their skin. Avoid applying the patch or gel to your breasts. Do not use estradiol if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. Talk to your doctor before taking any new medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements, as some (like St. John's Wort) can make estradiol less effective. Limit alcohol, as it may increase estradiol levels in your blood.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden chest pain or tightness, shortness of breath, sudden severe headache, vision changes, weakness or numbness on one side of your body (signs of stroke), pain or swelling in your legs (possible blood clot), yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), unusual vaginal bleeding, lumps in your breast, or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also contact your doctor if you notice skin irritation where you apply the patch or gel, if your symptoms are not improving, or if you have any concerns.
when_it_works: Many women start to notice some relief from hot flashes and night sweats within a few weeks of starting estradiol. Vaginal symptoms such as dryness or discomfort may take a bit longer — sometimes 4 to 8 weeks — to improve. The full benefit for bone protection may take several months. Keep taking your medication as prescribed even if you feel well. Talk to your doctor regularly about whether you still need this medication, as the goal is to use it at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time needed.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Do not use estradiol if you are pregnant. It can harm an unborn baby. BREASTFEEDING: Estradiol may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before using this medication if you are breastfeeding. OLDER ADULTS: Older women may have a higher risk of side effects such as blood clots, stroke, dementia, and breast cancer. Your doctor will carefully weigh the risks and benefits. LIVER PROBLEMS: Tell your doctor if you have liver disease, as estradiol may not be suitable for you or may require special monitoring. HISTORY OF CERTAIN CONDITIONS: Estradiol is generally NOT recommended if you have a history of breast cancer, uterine cancer, blood clots, stroke, or heart attack. Always give your doctor your full medical history before starting this medication.
